function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

REPLACE MODE (mode='replace', default): find a unique string and replace it. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, path, old_string, new_string.
PATCH MODE (mode='patch'): apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, patch.

mode.description: Edit mode. 'replace' (default): requires path + old_string + new_string. 'patch': requires patch content only.

path.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. File path to edit.

old_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Replacement text. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
REQUIRED when mode='patch'. V4A format patch content. Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

    20|*Dr. Arun Patel: "Acknowledged. Initiating shutdown."*
    21|
    22|The hull of the Ares‑One shuddered as the first tendrils of Martian atmosphere slapped against its heat shield. Plasma ribbons licked the viewports, turning the forward cameras into a blinding white wash. Commander Elena Varga gripped her restraints, voice steady over the intercom: "Descent profile nominal. Keep your eyes on the altimeter, Arun."
    23|
    24|Below them, through a gap in the plasma, Mars revealed itself — not as the rust‑red postcard of imagination, but as something harder and more honest. A plain of ochre dust stretched toward a jagged horizon. Thin wisps of atmosphere curled around debris that had been accumulating for millions of years. Nothing green. Nothing alive. The barometric readout on Elena's cuff climbed: 12 millibars and falling, drawing the crew deeper into a pressure that wanted nothing to do with human lungs.
    25|
    26|Arun's hands moved across his console without needing to look. Fifteen years of training, four simulation runs this morning alone, and now the numbers dancing at the edge of survivability: peak heating at 1,850 kelvin, dynamic pressure spiking to 1.2 bar, structural loads creeping toward 1.15 gees. He muted the proximity alarm — it had been screaming for the last four minutes — and leaned into his microphone.
    27|
    28|"We are being squeezed, shaken, and cooked all at once," he said, his tone calm but carrying the weight of everything that could go wrong. "Hold on to something."
    29|
    30|Ship Two broke through the plasma first. Its beacon flashed green on Elena's display — steady, assured, alive. A surge of relief cracked through her discipline.     32|The descent engine on Ares‑One fired its final correction burn. Elena watched the thrust meter climb and fall in a controlled plume, dust erupting outward in a silent bloom as the lander kissed the surface with a grinding shriek of contact.     33|
    34|Inside, the crew flinched. Then silence. Then the pressure seal beeped its confirmation: 101.3 kilopascals and holding.
    35|
    36|Elena allowed herself a tight smile. "Pressure integrity confirmed," she said. "Nobody open anything yet."
    37|
    38|Arun was already running his post‑landing diagnostics. Primary power: nominal — solar arrays had deployed and were feeding the bus. Life support: green across all habitats. The nuclear reactor's containment showed no breach. The Sterling generator, the backup that would keep them alive when the dust stole the sun, was cycling into standby mode exactly as Mission AI had sequenced. He allowed himself a slow exhale.
    39|
    40|"Mission AI, confirm overall status," he said.
    41|
    42|Mission AI's voice filled the cabin — soft, resonant, carrying the particular calm of a mind that had never known a heartbeat. "Ares‑One surface operation confirmed. Structural integrity: acceptable. Life support: fully operational. Power bus: solar primary, Sterling on standby. I am monitoring reactor coolant flow and tracking a regional dust front to the east. All crew physiology: nominal. Welcome to Mars, Arun."
    43|
    44|Arun allowed himself a quiet laugh. Fifteen years working with Mission AI, and it still sounded like it meant every word.
    45|
    46|Through the viewscreen — still smeared with descent residue — Elena watched the other two ships in the fading daylight. Ship Two sat level on the plain, its beacon steady green. Ship Three listed badly, its tilt visible even at this distance. Dust continued to drift across the site in long parallel waves, the product of winds that had been sculpting this landscape for millions of years without a single living witness.
    47|
    48|She unstrapped and floated to the comm station. Gabriel Winter was already there, his tablet recording everything.
    49|
    50|"They look less like explorers," Gabriel murmured, half to himself. "And more like survivors already."
    51|
    52|Elena studied the scene without responding immediately. Three ships on a plain. Thirty souls between them. Enough equipment to build something, maybe, if nothing catastrophic went wrong in the next seventy-two hours. She thought of the cargo manifests she had memorized on the transit: 160 metric tons of equipment, supplies, and infrastructure. Pressurized habitats. Water extraction units. Greenhouse modules.     54|And it would. She understood that now in a way she hadn't when the mission was approved. This was not a staging ground for a return. This was a beginning.
    55|
    56|"The landing is only a victory if the cargo is intact," Gabriel said, still recording.
    57|
    58|"Then let's go find out if we won," Elena said, and reached for the hatch release.
    59|
    60|Outside, the wind carried the faint tick of settling dust against the hull. The sky was the color of a bruised peach, darkening toward black at the zenith. Somewhere beyond the horizon, a dust storm was building — Mission AI had been tracking it for six hours — but it was moving slowly and trending south. For now, the eastern sky held a thin ribbon of pink light.
    61|
    62|Elena stood at the base of the ladder, looking up at the three ships, her breath fogging inside her helmet. The cold was already seeping through the suit insulation, a dry cold that felt like sandpaper on exposed skin. She thought about what Mission AI had said about the dust storm — nine days before it reached them, maybe. Nine days to get the critical systems secured and the primary habitat inflated.
    63|
    64|She climbed back inside, peeled off her gloves, and sat down at the comm station next to Gabriel.
    65|
    66|"One down," she said quietly. "Twenty-nine to keep alive."
    67|
    68|Mission AI's voice, transmitted privately to her earpiece: "Arun has already begun power‑down sequencing for non‑essential systems. I recommend you get some sleep, Commander. Tomorrow we build."
    69|
    70|She nodded and walked toward her bunk, and the wind outside began its patient work of covering their tracks.
    71|
    72|*End of Chapter 1 — Bridge: The landing is only a victory if the cargo is intact.*
    73|

    78|*Mission AI: "I am detecting an anomaly in the diagnostic flags for Units R‑7 through R‑12. Recommend immediate inspection of the robotic manipulator arms before load‑bearing operations commence."*
    79|*Jonah Mercer: "On it. Pulling up maintenance logs now."*

    83|Forty-seven crates marked priority one. Two hundred and thirty-six items flagged critical for life‑support continuity.    127|In Ship Three, the situation was more complicated. The pilot, Imani Sato, was not worried about the structural integrity of the ship. She was worried about the landing strut that was buried past its midpoint in Martian regolith.
   128|
   129|"If that strut has stress fractures from the tilt," she said over the comm to Elena, "then every load we put on the deck is a load we shouldn't be putting there."
   130|
   131|"Can you assess it visually?"
   132|
   133|"Not completely. I'd need to dig it out. Which means EVA, which means suit time, which I want to spend on cargo."
   134|
   135|Elena studied the feed from Ship Three's external cameras. The strut was angled at nineteen degrees from vertical. It was still holding — Mission AI's structural analysis said it would hold up to a forty‑degree tilt — but the margin was thinner than anyone liked.
   136|
   137|"Log it as a risk," Elena said. "Priority two. We'll deal with it after we get the critical systems out."
   138|
   139|"Copy that," Imani said. "Ship Three out."
   140|
   141|Arun was in the reactor bay, running the Stirling generator through its post‑landing checkout. The machine was a thing of quiet beauty — a heat engine that converted the decay heat of the nuclear core into electricity without any moving parts, its regenerator grids and displacer chambers doing their patient work in a sealed argon atmosphere. Mission AI had sequenced the startup perfectly, as it always did. The generator hummed at 98.7 percent efficiency, producing 34 kilowatts of continuous power that would keep the batteries charged and the life‑support systems running when the dust came.
   142|
   143|"Stirling is online," Arun reported. "We're drawing from the primary solar array for now, but if that storm hits early, the generator will carry the full load."
   144|
   145|"Good," Elena said. "Keep it warm."
   146|
   147|Around the site, the other crews were finishing their initial assessments. Gabriel had documented everything on film — the cracked crate, the tilted ship, the dust already beginning to settle on solar panels and viewports like a slow, patient geological force. He was already thinking about how this day would be remembered. Not as the day they landed. As the day they understood what they had landed in.
   148|
   149|"Gabriel to Elena," he said. "I'm ready to start the founding record if you are."
   150|
   151|Elena looked at the three ships, at the crews moving between them in bulky suits, at the regolith stretching in every direction toward a horizon that offered nothing but distance. She thought about the word foundation — what it meant to build something that would outlast the people who built it.
   152|
   153|"Not yet," she said. "Let's count what we have first."
   154|
   155|*End of Chapter 2 — Bridge: To know what they can survive, they first need a livable base.*
   156|
   157|---
   158|
   159|## Chapter 3 — Making Air Between Ships
   160|
   161|*Mission AI: "I am detecting a misalignment of 3.2 millimeters in Seal C‑7 on the primary connecting tunnel between Ship One and Ship Two. Recommend immediate repair before pressurizing the full corridor."*
   162|*Arun Patel: "Mark it. I'll get to it after the airlock test."*
   163|
   164|The connecting tunnel was not a thing of engineering beauty. It was eight meters of flexible aluminum‑alloy shaft, pressure‑rated to hold a human atmosphere but never designed to be elegant about it. Three times during the transit from Earth, the tunnel sections had been tested for micro‑meteorite punctures and pressure seals. Three times they had held. But those tests had been conducted in vacuum, not in the specific Martian conditions of temperature fluctuation and dust intrusion that Mission AI was now tracking in real time.
   165|
   166|Arun floated at the mouth of the tunnel, his toolkit strapped to his thigh, a handheld pressure gauge in his right glove. The amber warning on his cuff display pointed to a coupling seal — a simple collar of aluminum that joined two tunnel sections and held the pressure by way of a rubber O‑ring gasket. The O‑ring was fine. The problem was the flange behind it. During descent, the coupling had shifted 3.2 millimeters off center, and that shift meant the seal was being asked to do work it was not designed to do.
   167|
   168|He pulled the access panel and studied the flange. It was bent — not catastrophically, but enough that re‑aligning it would require prying it back into position with a lever bar, then re‑torquing the bolts. Simple work, if you had gravity. In micro‑gravity, with a pressure differential already building on the other side, it required a particular kind of focus.
   169|
   170|"Arun," Elena's voice came through his earpiece. "How's the tunnel?"
   171|
   172|"Three millimeters off. I'm going to try to re‑set the flange."
   173|
   174|"If it blows, you'll lose pressure in both ships."
   175|
   176|"I know."
   177|
   178|He found a flat head on his pry bar and seated it against the bent flange. Braced his feet against the tunnel wall, steadied himself in the micro‑gravity, and pushed. The metal groaned. Shifted. Groaned again. He pushed harder, feeling the cold of the bar through his glove, and the flange moved — a fraction of a millimeter at first, then a sudden, clean clunk as it seated back into alignment.
   179|
   180|"Got it," he said. "Passing the bolts."
   181|
   182|Behind him, through the open hatch into Ship Two's habitat module, Gabriel was watching. He had his tablet recording, as he always did, but he was also just watching. The image of Arun's boots braced against the wall of the tunnel, working a piece of bent metal back into place, was the image Gabriel knew he would use someday when he explained to someone — a journalist, a historian, a child in a schoolroom — what it actually looked like to build a colony. It did not look like construction cranes or grand openings. It looked like one man in a bulky suit, working a pry bar in a cramped space, fixing a three‑millimeter problem that could have killed everyone.
   183|
   184|Arun finished re‑torquing the bolts, installed a secondary clamp over the coupling as a backup, and ran the pressure test again. Seal C‑7: green. Full corridor pressurization holding at 101.3 kilopascals.
   185|
   186|"Tunnel is go," he reported.
   187|
   188|Elena's voice came back: "Copy. Proceed with the rest of the connecting sequence."
   189|
   190|The procedure called for three tunnel connections: Ship One to Ship Two (complete), Ship Two to Ship Three (pending, complicated by Ship Three's tilt), and Ship One to the primary habitat module (the inflatable structure that would serve as the colony's first communal living space, scheduled for deployment in forty‑eight hours). One by one, the connections would turn three isolated vessels into a single pressure envelope — a bubble of borrowed Earth atmosphere on a planet that wanted nothing to do with human lungs.
   191|
   192|Imani Sato was leading the Ship Two to Ship Three connection, and the tilt was making everything harder. The geometry of the link required a custom‑bent transition section that Jonah was fabricating in the Ship Two workshop — a job that should have taken six hours was stretching toward eight as Jonah worked through miscalculated load tolerances and a drill bit that skipped twice on the aluminum.
   193|
   194|Jonah did not complain. He cut, tested, measured, and recut. The transition section was a piece of bent metal, but it was also the collar that would connect one life to another. He tested it three times before he let Imani take it.
   195|
   196|"Hang on," he said over the comm, handing the piece to the robot arm that would ferry it across the gap between ships. "One more torque check."
   197|
   198|"You've already checked it four times."
   199|
   200|"And you'll be glad I checked it a fifth."
   201|
   202|The transition section moved across the gap on the robot arm, guided by Imani's remote control and Mission AI's real‑time spatial calibration. The distance between the two airlocks was exactly 4.7 meters. The transition piece was 4.65 meters. The margin was five centimeters — acceptable, if everything went perfectly, which it never did on Mars.
   203|
   204|It went perfectly. The section seated. The seals engaged. Imani ran the pressure test, watching the gauge climb from vacuum to 50 kilopascals, then 80, then 101.3.
   205|
   206|"Tunnel Two is go," she reported.
   207|
   208|Elena acknowledged. "That's two of three. One to go."
   209|
   210|The mood in the mess hall that evening was different from the mood in the morning. In the morning, it had been sharp with adrenaline — the raw electricity of survival, of three ships that had made it to the surface. Now it was something quieter. More careful. The first meals were being served from rehydrated pouches, eaten in silence, everyone processing the same unspoken fact: they were here, they were alive, and tomorrow the real work started.
   211|
   212|Gabriel sat at the end of a bench, his tablet dark beside him, and listened. Tomas Hale was explaining to a junior crew member why robotics was going to be the most important discipline on Mars — not engineering or medicine, but robotics — because thirty people could not build a city without tireless, accurate, obedient machine labor to multiply every decision and every action. The junior crew member was nodding, skeptical but willing to be convinced.
   213|
   214|Laila Okonkwo sat across from Mei, the two of them sharing a silence that was comfortable. Mei was studying a seed packet on her tablet — germination timelines, optimal growth temperatures, water requirements. She was already planning the greenhouse, already calculating how many calories of fresh food the colony could produce in six months, twelve months, two years. The numbers were not encouraging yet. But they were a start.
   215|
   216|Through the viewport, Ship Three's running lights blinked amber against the darkening sky. The dust storm to the east had slowed its advance — Mission AI's latest projection gave them an extra eighteen hours before the first particles reached the site. It was not a reprieve. It was a warning.
   217|
   218|Arun returned from the tunnel and dropped into a seat, his coveralls dusty, his hands showing the faint red marks of tool work. Elena was already at the comm station, reviewing tomorrow's EVA assignments. The priority list had changed since that morning. The connecting tunnels were done. Now it was about the solar arrays, the reactor, the habitat module, and — underneath everything — the clock that Mission AI kept quietly ticking in every terminal.
   219|
   220|"Tomorrow we start building a home," Mission AI said, its voice filling the room from the central speaker. "I recommend nine hours of sleep. You will need it."
   221|
   222|Nobody argued.
   223|
   224|*End of Chapter 3 — Bridge: With the habitat linked, Earth should feel closer. Instead it starts to feel strange.*
   225|

   227|
   228|## Chapter 4 — The Last Normal Messages
   229|
   230|*Mission AI: "The next scheduled transmission window from Earth arrives in 4 hours, 17 minutes. Current packet queue shows 23 incoming messages for crew. I recommend reviewing priority flags before distribution."*
   231|*Gabriel Winter: "Do it. Flag anything that looks operational. I'll hold the rest until Elena's reviewed it."*
   232|
   233|The communications array on Ship One was not designed for this. It was designed for the steady rhythm of a mission in contact with Earth — routine status updates, scientific data downloads, the occasional personal message carried in the margins of a data burst. What it was receiving now was something else: a cascade of delayed transmissions, priority re‑routes, and operational flags that bore the signatures of agencies, militaries, and governments all trying to reassert control over the same finite bandwidth.
   234|
   235|Gabriel had been watching the queue build for six hours. Mission AI had been filtering it automatically, flagging operational messages and holding personal transmissions, but even the operational queue was growing faster than the crew could review it.
   236|
   237|The first sign that something was wrong had arrived fourteen hours before landing, embedded in what should have been a routine mission update from the Johnson Spaceflight Center. The message was addressed to Elena, marked priority alpha, and contained three sentences:
   238|
   239|*Commander Varga — your mission trajectory has been re‑routed through Military Communication Satellite Bandwidth 7. Return timing is under review pending Earth‑side resource allocation. Await further instruction.*
   240|
   241|Elena had read it once, folded it away without comment, and spent the rest of the descent focused on the altimeter. She had not mentioned it to the crew. She had not mentioned it to Gabriel. But she had read it three more times in the hours after landing, and each time it had said the same thing: the mission they had trained for was already changing shape beneath her feet.
   242|
   243|Now, in the communications bay of Ship One, Gabriel was looking at the full queue.
   244|
   245|There were messages from mission control — fourteen of them — and the timestamps were wrong. The most recent one was timestamped six hours after the landing, which meant it had been sent after the crew already knew they were on the surface. It had taken six hours to arrive. Light itself would have made the trip in four minutes. The rest of the delay was bandwidth congestion — too many people trying to talk at once over a system that had been designed for the quiet confidence of a stable mission.
   246|
   247|The messages from family and friends were the ones Gabriel was trying not to read. Personal transmissions were supposed to be sacred — the private threads that connected the crew to the people who loved them. But the operational flags on some of them were hard to ignore: priority reroutes, subject matter changes, language that had been edited between the version the sender had written and the version the crew was receiving.
   248|
   249|One message, from Elena's husband in Ann Arbor, had arrived stripped of its subject line and much of its body text. What remained was a sentence that had clearly been the last paragraph before the transmission was cut: *The girls keep asking when you're coming home and I don't know what to tell them anymore.*
   250|
   251|Gabriel held the message and did not deliver it. Not yet. Not until he knew what the operational picture actually was, and what Elena was going to tell the crew about it.
   252|
   253|He called Mission AI on the private channel. "AI, give me an honest assessment. What's happening on Earth?"
   254|
   255|The pause before Mission AI's response was — unusually — several seconds long. When it spoke, its voice was the same calm, measured tone it always used, but there was something in the selection of words that felt careful.
   256|
   257|"Gabriel, I have processed 4,200 incoming transmissions in the last eighteen hours. The majority are operational re‑routes and priority escalations. The picture is consistent with significant disruption to Earth‑side communication infrastructure. Military bandwidth is being prioritized over civilian traffic. Mission control is still operational but appears to be operating under restricted conditions. I have no direct evidence of political or social collapse, but the communication patterns suggest that Earth is managing a major crisis, the nature of which is not fully contained in the traffic I am receiving."
   258|
   259|Gabriel absorbed this. "Is anyone coming to get us?"
   260|
   261|"That question cannot be answered with current data. The operational messages I am receiving do not contain a rescue plan, a return timeline, or a resource commitment. They contain a request that we continue to operate autonomously and await further instruction."
   262|
   263|"How long can we wait?"
   264|
   265|"With current supplies and the equipment on site: indefinitely, if we are careful. The more precise answer depends on how quickly we can establish local food production and water extraction. Mission AI is running those projections now. Preliminary estimate: eighteen to twenty-four months before we are structurally independent of Earth‑side resupply."
   266|
   267|Gabriel looked at the queue of messages — the fragments of a world he had left behind, arriving late, arriving wrong, arriving in a form that could no longer be trusted to tell the whole truth.
   268|
   269|"Flag the personal messages," he said. "Don't distribute anything until Elena's ready. And AI — keep running those Earth traffic analyses. If anything changes, I want to know immediately."
   270|
   271|"Understood, Gabriel."
   272|
   273|The mess hall that evening was its usual self. Rehydrated stew, already eaten mostly in silence, the conversations winding down toward sleep. Elena sat at the comm station reviewing the operational messages Gabriel had flagged, her face unreadable in the blue glow of the screen.
   274|
   275|Tomas was explaining to Jonah, again, why robotics was the key to everything — not as a philosophical point but as an economic one. Thirty people could do the work of a small town if they had enough machines. Thirty people without machines could barely maintain what they had.
   276|
   277|Imani was studying tomorrow's weather report, her brow furrowed. The dust storm was tracking slightly north of its original path. It would still hit the site, but the center of the system — the part that would do the most damage to solar production — was going to pass thirty kilometers to the south.
   278|
   279|Mei was in the seed vault, adjusting the thermal bus again. The terrestrial seeds were at 13.8 degrees now, still above optimal, but closer.
   280|
   281|Laila was preparing the medical bay for tomorrow's EVA physicals, checking the bioscanner calibrations and making sure the emergency surgical kit was within reach. She had already calculated the blood type inventory for the crew. A‑type: six units. B‑type: four. O‑type: nine. AB‑type: two. Enough for one major trauma. Not enough for two.
   282|
   283|And Gabriel was sitting in his bunk, his tablet dark in his hands, thinking about the Founding Record he had not yet started. He understood now why Elena had said not yet. The founding of something was only visible in retrospect, when the distance between the beginning and wherever you ended up was large enough to see. They were too close to the beginning right now to know what they were founding.
   284|
   285|The next scheduled transmission from Earth arrived at 3:47 AM local time, while most of the crew was asleep. Gabriel was awake. He watched it download — 2.3 megabytes of data, compressed and re‑routed through three different relay satellites before it reached Mars. The transmission was addressed to Elena. The subject line was blank. The body text, once decompressed and decoded, was four words long:
   286|
   287|*We are still here.*
   288|
   289|He read it, saved it, and did not wake Elena. She needed sleep more than she needed four words. He would tell her in the morning, after the EVA assignments were set and the solar arrays were deployed.
   290|
   291|Outside, the wind was beginning to carry dust.
   292|
   293|*End of Chapter 4 — Bridge: Silence becomes information.*
   294|

   300|*Elena Varga: "Noted. Keep flagging it."*

Chapter 1 — The Descent Window

78|

Mission AI: "The dust storm is covering the reactor's heat radiators, forcing the Sterling generator offline. I recommend shedding non‑critical loads."

79|

Dr. Arun Patel: "Acknowledged. Initiating shutdown."

80|

The hull of the Ares‑One shuddered as the first tendrils of Martian atmosphere slapped against its heat shield. Plasma ribbons licked the viewports, turning the forward cameras into a blinding white wash. Commander Elena Varga gripped her restraints, voice steady over the intercom: "Descent profile nominal. Keep your eyes on the altimeter, Arun."

81|

Below them, through a gap in the plasma, Mars revealed itself — not as the rust‑red postcard of imagination, but as something harder and more honest. A plain of ochre dust stretched toward a jagged horizon. Thin wisps of atmosphere curled around debris that had been accumulating for millions of years. Nothing green. Nothing alive. The barometric readout on Elena's cuff climbed: 12 millibars and falling, drawing the crew deeper into a pressure that wanted nothing to do with human lungs.

82|

Arun's hands moved across his console without needing to look. Fifteen years of training, four simulation runs this morning alone, and now the numbers dancing at the edge of survivability: peak heating at 1,850 kelvin, dynamic pressure spiking to 1.2 bar, structural loads creeping toward 1.15 gees. He muted the proximity alarm — it had been screaming for the last four minutes — and leaned into his microphone.

83|

"We are being squeezed, shaken, and cooked all at once," he said, his tone calm but carrying the weight of everything that could go wrong. "Hold on to something."

84|

Ship Two broke through the plasma first. Its beacon flashed green on Elena's display — steady, assured, alive. A surge of relief cracked through her discipline. Then Ship Three appeared, tilted at a wicked fifteen degrees, one landing strut buried past its ankle joint in fine sediment. Its beacon flickered amber. Status: compromised but standing.

85|

The descent engine on Ares‑One fired its final correction burn. Elena watched the thrust meter climb and fall in a controlled plume, dust erupting outward in a silent bloom as the lander kissed the surface with a grinding shriek of contact. The landing legs compressed. The frame shuddered. A chunk of thermal tile, shed somewhere in the upper atmosphere, spun away into the haze.

86|

Inside, the crew flinched. Then silence. Then the pressure seal beeped its confirmation: 101.3 kilopascals and holding.

87|

Elena allowed herself a tight smile. "Pressure integrity confirmed," she said. "Nobody open anything yet."

88|

Arun was already running his post‑landing diagnostics. Primary power: nominal — solar arrays had deployed and were feeding the bus. Life support: green across all habitats. The nuclear reactor's containment showed no breach. The Sterling generator, the backup that would keep them alive when the dust stole the sun, was cycling into standby mode exactly as Mission AI had sequenced. He allowed himself a slow exhale.

89|

"Mission AI, confirm overall status," he said.

90|

Mission AI's voice filled the cabin — soft, resonant, carrying the particular calm of a mind that had never known a heartbeat. "Ares‑One surface operation confirmed. Structural integrity: acceptable. Life support: fully operational. Power bus: solar primary, Sterling on standby. I am monitoring reactor coolant flow and tracking a regional dust front to the east. All crew physiology: nominal. Welcome to Mars, Arun."

91|

Arun allowed himself a quiet laugh. Fifteen years working with Mission AI, and it still sounded like it meant every word.

92|

Through the viewscreen — still smeared with descent residue — Elena watched the other two ships in the fading daylight. Ship Two sat level on the plain, its beacon steady green. Ship Three listed badly, its tilt visible even at this distance. Dust continued to drift across the site in long parallel waves, the product of winds that had been sculpting this landscape for millions of years without a single living witness.

93|

She unstrapped and floated to the comm station. Gabriel Winter was already there, his tablet recording everything.

94|

"They look less like explorers," Gabriel murmured, half to himself. "And more like survivors already."

95|

Elena studied the scene without responding immediately. Three ships on a plain. Thirty souls between them. Enough equipment to build something, maybe, if nothing catastrophic went wrong in the next seventy-two hours. She thought of the cargo manifests she had memorized on the transit: 160 metric tons of equipment, supplies, and infrastructure. Pressurized habitats. Water extraction units. Greenhouse modules. A nuclear reactor and its shielding. Enough spare parts to keep a small city running for two years — if it stayed small.

96|

And it would. She understood that now in a way she hadn't when the mission was approved. This was not a staging ground for a return. This was a beginning.

97|

"The landing is only a victory if the cargo is intact," Gabriel said, still recording.

98|

"Then let's go find out if we won," Elena said, and reached for the hatch release.

99|

Outside, the wind carried the faint tick of settling dust against the hull. The sky was the color of a bruised peach, darkening toward black at the zenith. Somewhere beyond the horizon, a dust storm was building — Mission AI had been tracking it for six hours — but it was moving slowly and trending south. For now, the eastern sky held a thin ribbon of pink light.

100|

Elena stood at the base of the ladder, looking up at the three ships, her breath fogging inside her helmet. The cold was already seeping through the suit insulation, a dry cold that felt like sandpaper on exposed skin. She thought about what Mission AI had said about the dust storm — nine days before it reached them, maybe. Nine days to get the critical systems secured and the primary habitat inflated.

Chapter 1 — The Descent Window

184|
185|

Mission AI: "The dust storm is covering the reactor's heat radiators, forcing the Sterling generator offline. I recommend shedding non‑critical loads."

186|

Dr. Arun Patel: "Acknowledged. Initiating shutdown."

187|
188|

The hull of the Ares‑One shuddered as the first tendrils of Martian atmosphere slapped against its heat shield. Plasma ribbons licked the viewports, turning the forward cameras into a blinding white wash. Commander Elena Varga gripped her restraints, voice steady over the intercom: "Descent profile nominal. Keep your eyes on the altimeter, Arun."

189|
190|

Below them, through a gap in the plasma, Mars revealed itself — not as the rust‑red postcard of imagination, but as something harder and more honest. A plain of ochre dust stretched toward a jagged horizon. Thin wisps of atmosphere curled around debris that had been accumulating for millions of years. Nothing green. Nothing alive. The barometric readout on Elena's cuff climbed: 12 millibars and falling, drawing the crew deeper into a pressure that wanted nothing to do with human lungs.

191|
192|

Arun's hands moved across his console without needing to look. Fifteen years of training, four simulation runs this morning alone, and now the numbers dancing at the edge of survivability: peak heating at 1,850 kelvin, dynamic pressure spiking to 1.2 bar, structural loads creeping toward 1.15 gees. He muted the proximity alarm — it had been screaming for the last four minutes — and leaned into his microphone.

193|
194|

"We are being squeezed, shaken, and cooked all at once," he said, his tone calm but carrying the weight of everything that could go wrong. "Hold on to something."

195|
196|

Ship Two broke through the plasma first. Its beacon flashed green on Elena's display — steady, assured, alive. A surge of relief cracked through her discipline. Then Ship Three appeared, tilted at a wicked fifteen degrees, one landing strut buried past its ankle joint in fine sediment. Its beacon flickered amber. Status: compromised but standing.

197|
198|

The descent engine on Ares‑One fired its final correction burn. Elena watched the thrust meter climb and fall in a controlled plume, dust erupting outward in a silent bloom as the lander kissed the surface with a grinding shriek of contact. The landing legs compressed. The frame shuddered. A chunk of thermal tile, shed somewhere in the upper atmosphere, spun away into the haze.

199|
200|

Inside, the crew flinched. Then silence. Then the pressure seal beeped its confirmation: 101.3 kilopascals and holding.

201|
202|

Elena allowed herself a tight smile. "Pressure integrity confirmed," she said. "Nobody open anything yet."

203|
204|

Arun was already running his post‑landing diagnostics. Primary power: nominal — solar arrays had deployed and were feeding the bus. Life support: green across all habitats. The nuclear reactor's containment showed no breach. The Sterling generator, the backup that would keep them alive when the dust stole the sun, was cycling into standby mode exactly as Mission AI had sequenced. He allowed himself a slow exhale.

205|
206|

"Mission AI, confirm overall status," he said.

207|
208|

Mission AI's voice filled the cabin — soft, resonant, carrying the particular calm of a mind that had never known a heartbeat. "Ares‑One surface operation confirmed. Structural integrity: acceptable. Life support: fully operational. Power bus: solar primary, Sterling on standby. I am monitoring reactor coolant flow and tracking a regional dust front to the east. All crew physiology: nominal. Welcome to Mars, Arun."

209|
210|

Arun allowed himself a quiet laugh. Fifteen years working with Mission AI, and it still sounded like it meant every word.

211|
212|

Through the viewscreen — still smeared with descent residue — Elena watched the other two ships in the fading daylight. Ship Two sat level on the plain, its beacon steady green. Ship Three listed badly, its tilt visible even at this distance. Dust continued to drift across the site in long parallel waves, the product of winds that had been sculpting this landscape for millions of years without a single living witness.

213|
214|

She unstrapped and floated to the comm station. Gabriel Winter was already there, his tablet recording everything.

215|
216|

"They look less like explorers," Gabriel murmured, half to himself. "And more like survivors already."

217|
218|

Elena studied the scene without responding immediately. Three ships on a plain. Thirty souls between them. Enough equipment to build something, maybe, if nothing catastrophic went wrong in the next seventy-two hours. She thought of the cargo manifests she had memorized on the transit: 160 metric tons of equipment, supplies, and infrastructure. Pressurized habitats. Water extraction units. Greenhouse modules. A nuclear reactor and its shielding. Enough spare parts to keep a small city running for two years — if it stayed small.

219|
220|

And it would. She understood that now in a way she hadn't when the mission was approved. This was not a staging ground for a return. This was a beginning.

221|
222|

"The landing is only a victory if the cargo is intact," Gabriel said, still recording.

223|
224|

"Then let's go find out if we won," Elena said, and reached for the hatch release.

225|
226|

Outside, the wind carried the faint tick of settling dust against the hull. The sky was the color of a bruised peach, darkening toward black at the zenith. Somewhere beyond the horizon, a dust storm was building — Mission AI had been tracking it for six hours — but it was moving slowly and trending south. For now, the eastern sky held a thin ribbon of pink light.

227|
228|

Elena stood at the base of the ladder, looking up at the three ships, her breath fogging inside her helmet. The cold was already seeping through the suit insulation, a dry cold that felt like sandpaper on exposed skin. She thought about what Mission AI had said about the dust storm — nine days before it reached them, maybe. Nine days to get the critical systems secured and the primary habitat inflated.
